sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH), historically termed Pseudotumor Cerebri, is a syndrome characterized by increased intracranial pressure (ICP) of unknown etiology. It primarily affects overweight women of childbearing age. The diagnosis requires the absence of a space-occupying lesion, normal CSF composition, and documented elevated opening pressure on lumbar puncture.

rows: Increased ICP (Headache, Papilledema, CN VI palsy)
No focal deficits except abducens nerve palsy
Normal brain parenchyma; No mass, hydrocephalus, or thrombosis
No other identifiable cause of intracranial hypertension

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptomatology
content: Headache (90%): Typically worse in the morning or with Valsalva
Transient Visual Obscurations (TVOs): Lasting seconds, usually postural
Pulsatile Tinnitus: 'Whooshing' sound synchronous with pulse
Diplopia: Horizontal, usually due to unilateral or bilateral CN VI palsy
Photopsia: Flashing lights without retinal pathology
Radicular pain: Neck and back pain common

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Papilledema: Often bilateral and symmetric, but can be asymmetric
Paton's Lines: Circumferential peripapillary retinal folds
Enlarged Blind Spot: On Goldmann or Humphrey visual fields
Peripheral Constriction: Most common field defect (nasal step/arcuate)
Loss of Spontaneous Venous Pulsation (SVP): Present in only 80% of normal people
Sixth Nerve Palsy: False localizing sign due to ICP

rows: C-shaped halo of edema, temporal disc margin spared
Circumferential halo; elevation of nasal border
Obscuration of one or more major retinal vessels at disc margin
Total obscuration of a major vessel on the disc
Dome-shaped protrusion; total obscuration of all vessels; Paton lines

sections.title: Neuroimaging Markers (MRI/MRV)
content: Empty Sella Turcica (most sensitive but not specific)
Posterior globe flattening
Optic nerve sheath distension (>5.9mm)
Optic nerve tortuosity
Transverse venous sinus stenosis (best seen on MRV)
Slit-like ventricles (less common)

sections.title: Secondary Causes (The 'P's & 'T's)
content: Tetracyclines (Minocycline, Doxycycline)
Vitamin A Excess (Isotretinoin, Retinoids)
Thyroid Dysregulation
Triamcinolone/Steroid Withdrawal
Oral Contraceptives / Progestins
Growth Hormone Replacement
Sleep Apnea

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Weight Loss (Target 6-10% of total body weight)
Step 2: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (Acetazolamide 500mg BID, titrate up to 4g/day)
Step 3: Alternative Medical Therapy (Topiramate - also aids weight loss and headaches)
Step 4: Diuretics (Furosemide as adjunctive therapy)
Step 5: Serial Visual Fields and OCT to monitor RNFL thickness

sections.title: Surgical & Interventional Options
content: Optic Nerve Sheath Decompression (ONSD): Best for progressive visual loss despite meds
CSF Shunting (LP or VP Shunt): Best for severe headache + visual loss
Venous Sinus Stenting: Emerging for patients with severe stenosis (transverse/sigmoid)
Bariatric Surgery: Highly effective for long-term remission in morbidly obese

content.explanation: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Treatment Trial: Proved Acetazolamide + Low Sodium Weight-Reduction Diet significantly improves visual field function, papilledema grade, and quality of life compared to diet alone in mild visual loss cases.

sections.title: Visual Red Flags: Fulminant IIH
content: Rapidly progressive vision loss over days (Fulminant IIH)
New-onset Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD)
Severe disc pallor (Atrophy) following chronic edema
High-grade papilledema with macular exudates/hemorrhage
Refractory headache unresponsive to maximum medical therapy

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Practice
content: Always check blood pressure to rule out Malignant Hypertension.
OCT RNFL is useful for monitoring, but be wary of 'pseudo-improvement' when edema resolves into atrophy.
In pregnancy: Weight management and Acetazolamide (after 20 weeks) are generally considered safe; avoid aggressive weight loss during gestation.
Lumbar puncture is both diagnostic and therapeutic (temporary relief), but should only be done AFTER imaging to rule out mass.
